cards.title: Dimension-preserving search-to-decision reductions for SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction that, using only \(\gamma\)-GapSVP queries on lattices of the same dimension \(n\), solves SVP with approximation factor polynomial in \(n\) and \(\gamma\)? Concretely, do there exist absolute positive integers \(C,a,b\) and one randomized oracle machine \(R\) such that for every \(n\ge1\), every nonsingular \(B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\), every rational \(\gamma\ge1\), and every admissible oracle \(O_\gamma\) below, \(R^{O_\gamma}(B,\gamma)\) runs in at most \(C(N+2)^b\) steps and outputs \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\setminus\{0\}\) with \[ \Pr\!\left[\|Bz\|_2\le C(n\gamma)^a\lambda_1(L(B))\right]\ge2/3? \] Here \(N\) is the bit length of the encoded input, and the probability is over the reduction’s random bits.
cards.why: Search returns a short lattice vector, whereas a decision oracle only certifies which side of a length gap the lattice lies on. Bridging these versions with polynomial approximation loss and no dimension increase would sharpen a basic computational relationship at the center of lattice algorithms and worst-case hardness assumptions in cryptography.
cards.status_note: The target is explicitly open in Bennett’s 24 January 2023 source. The near-exact 2016 theorem and the older reduction-map convention were checked directly, as were the dated June 2022 workshop questions. Bounded later searches through 14 September 2026 located no verified matching same-dimension classical reduction with polynomial loss. Recent LWE/LPN search-to-decision results concern different average-case problems and were not treated as resolutions. This is a limited source review, not exhaustive current-status or Lean proof certification.

sentences: The input is a rational lattice basis, and the search task is to produce a nonzero vector whose length approximates the shortest possible length.
The available oracle only distinguishes short-vector lengths across a multiplicative gap.
The question asks for a classical polynomial-time reduction that keeps every query in the original dimension and loses only a polynomial in dimension and approximation factor.
Known exact and near-exact reductions do not supply this guarantee across the full approximation range.
A resolution would clarify whether approximate lattice decision algorithms can be converted efficiently into search algorithms without an exponential dimensional penalty.

cards.definitions:
The input lattice is \(L(B)=\{Bz:z\in\mathbb Z^n\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with a rational full-rank square basis whose columns generate it. The Euclidean norm is \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\lambda_1(L)=\min\{\|v\|_2:v\in L,\ v\ne0\}\). The output is an exact integer coefficient vector \(z\), so its nonzero lattice vector is unambiguously represented even when coordinates are rational. There is no norm other than \(\ell_2\), target point, uniqueness promise, preprocessing of a fixed lattice, or ideal-lattice restriction.

An oracle query is \((\widetilde B,r)\), where \(\widetilde B\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and \(r\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\). An admissible \(O_\gamma\) is any total Boolean function on these valid queries satisfying \[ \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=1,\qquad \lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))>\gamma r\implies O_\gamma(\widetilde B,r)=0.\] When \(r<\lambda_1(L(\widetilde B))\le\gamma r\), its answer can be either bit. The reduction must succeed for every such total completion of the promise problem, including completions with no computability assumption. Repeated identical queries have the same answer because the oracle is a function. The same input value \(\gamma\) applies to every query. At \(\gamma=1\) there is no gap.

Dimension preservation means every oracle lattice has exactly the original dimension \(n\), including its ambient dimension and rank. Queries may use different bases and thresholds, but cannot increase dimension even by an additive constant. This follows the explicit same-\(n\) statement of Open Problem 4.5. Adaptively chosen queries are allowed; this is a Cook (oracle Turing) reduction, not a requirement of one nonadaptive query.

Integers, rational numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary with signs and delimiters; \(N\) includes the entire basis and \(\gamma\). Use a probabilistic multitape oracle Turing machine with independent unbiased coin flips, a read-only input tape, work tapes and a query tape. Writing a query and reading its one-bit answer are charged; the oracle itself returns that bit in one oracle step. All arithmetic is implemented on binary tapes and pays its full bit cost. The displayed polynomial bounds total time on every random tape and every admissible oracle, and therefore bounds the number and bit lengths of queries and output. Only valid full-rank rational queries are allowed. There is no additional oracle, advice, quantum computation, or free real arithmetic.

The constants and the finite program are fixed before \(n,B,\gamma\) and the oracle are chosen. A bound \(C(n\gamma)^a\) expresses an unspecified polynomial loss uniformly over the domain \(n,\gamma\ge1\); replacing it by any fixed polynomial in these two parameters gives the same polynomial-loss existence target after increasing \(C,a\). The chosen reduction is allowed bounded-error randomness. This makes explicit the classical randomized reduction convention used by the cited near-exact results, rather than adding a deterministic-only requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a reduction and uniform polynomial bounds exist, with correctness against every admissible completion of the promise oracle, or prove their nonexistence. A positive result must bound the output norm, bit complexity, and dimension of every query. Preserving dimension only up to an unbounded factor, obtaining an approximation loss exponential in \(n\), assuming special lattices, or giving only a quantum reduction does not meet the target. The known exact case or approximation factors approaching one alone do not establish the quantified statement.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for polynomial loss in the approximation factor, not exact preservation of that factor. It also explicitly retains dimension. This matters for lattice algorithms whose costs depend exponentially on dimension, and for distinguishing an algorithm that recognizes short vectors from one that actually finds them.

The search and decision versions are known to be equivalent under dimension-preserving reductions in the exact case \(\gamma=1\). The 2016 randomized reduction has search loss \(\gamma^{n/s}\) and running time \(2^{O(s)}\gamma^{O(n)}\), for \(s\ge\log(n+1)\), with input-bit polynomial factors suppressed in that summary. Choosing \(s\) logarithmic gives an efficient useful guarantee when \(\gamma\) is very close to one; it does not give a polynomial-loss polynomial-time reduction for all approximation factors.

Bennett’s 2023 problem is phrased using rational square bases and Euclidean length. The older reduction map uses a relaxed convention that permits an additive constant in dimension, while the card follows the later explicit same-dimension wording. The distinction is recorded so that a looser reduction is not silently counted as satisfying the target.

The source relates a solution at polynomial approximation factors to worst-case search-SVP foundations for lattice cryptography. The Simons list also discusses search-to-decision questions for closest vectors and independent short vectors, including quantum variants. Those questions have different outputs, oracles or computational models and do not settle the reduction here.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
